Newborn Care

Kidney dysplasia in babies: development, function and care

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Kidney dysplasia means that part or all of a kidney developed abnormally before birth. It can affect one or both kidneys, with very different effects on function. A scan finding needs a clear explanation and a follow-up plan; it does not automatically mean that both kidneys will fail or that a parent caused the problem.

What the kidneys and urinary tract normally do

The kidneys remove waste and extra water from blood and help balance salts and control blood pressure. Their tiny filtering units contain a filter and a tubule that returns needed substances to the body. Urine passes through the ureters to the bladder, where it is stored, and leaves through the urethra when the bladder empties.

Kidneys develop through coordinated growth and branching of different tissues before birth. In dysplasia, the internal tissue is disorganized and there are fewer normally formed working units. This is different from saying that every affected kidney simply has trapped urine. Urine drainage problems can coexist, but need their own assessment.

Dysplasia is a spectrum, not another name for every cystic kidney

A dysplastic kidney may be small, partly affected or have cysts; some useful function can remain. Multicystic dysplastic kidney, or MCDK, is a severe cystic form with little or no useful function in that kidney. Other conditions, including a small but more normally structured kidney, an absent kidney and inherited polycystic kidney disease, are different diagnoses.

If only one kidney is affected and the other is healthy, overall function is often adequate. When both are dysplastic, some babies initially have enough function and may remain well for years; others have serious impairment early. The exact tissue, other urinary findings and measured function matter more than a single label. Reported frequency varies with definitions and detection, so one old incidence estimate cannot describe every form.

Possible causes and family questions

Often the precise cause is unknown. Genetic changes can sometimes explain isolated kidney dysplasia or a wider condition affecting other organs. The team considers family kidney problems, hearing or eye findings and other developmental differences. Genetic counselling and testing are particularly relevant for familial, syndromic or bilateral disease; a result does not always predict how well the kidneys will work.

Some medicine or drug exposures during pregnancy are associated with abnormal kidney development, but a diagnosis does not prove that a particular exposure caused it. Review exact products and dates with the pregnancy and prescribing teams. Do not abruptly stop necessary seizure or blood-pressure treatment yourself. There is no guaranteed prevention method, and the finding is not evidence of parental fault. Future-pregnancy advice depends on the actual diagnosis and family assessment.

Symptoms and complications are variable

Many babies with one dysplastic kidney have no obvious symptoms. High blood pressure, protein in urine or reduced filtering function may also be silent. Urinary infection can cause fever, feeding changes, vomiting or urinary discomfort. Some enlarged cystic kidneys cause a lump or discomfort, but an enlarged painful kidney is not a feature of every case.

Reduced function can become more apparent as a child grows, especially when both kidneys are affected. Dysplasia describes development; it does not mean that a baby has cancer. If you are concerned about a cancer-risk statement or an uncertain mass on a scan, ask the specialist to explain the exact finding. A general risk claim is not, by itself, a reason to remove a kidney or assume that cancer is present.

What a pregnancy scan can and cannot show

An ultrasound around the mid-pregnancy screening visit may suggest dysplasia, although some cases are found later. The specialist assesses both kidneys, their size and internal appearance, any cysts, the bladder, urinary drainage, other organs and amniotic fluid. Further scans can clarify an uncertain finding and help plan birth and care afterwards.

Fetal urine contributes to amniotic fluid, which supports lung development. Very low fluid with severe bilateral kidney disease can signal serious breathing and kidney problems after birth. Ultrasound cannot give a guaranteed personal prognosis or identify every genetic cause. Ask what diagnosis is most likely, what remains uncertain and whether fetal-medicine and paediatric kidney specialists should review the pregnancy together.

Confirming the diagnosis and choosing extra tests

After birth, ultrasound checks kidney structure, growth and the urinary tract. Blood tests estimate overall kidney function and salt balance; urine tests can check protein or infection. A baby's age and clinical condition affect interpretation. Kidney dysplasia is usually diagnosed clinically from imaging and assessment: a biopsy is not routinely needed just to prove the label.

A bladder contrast test such as a VCUG or MCUG may investigate suspected reflux or an outlet problem. Selected DMSA or MAG3 nuclear scans answer questions about tissue, function or drainage. These tests are not an automatic package for every child, particularly when ultrasound shows no urinary-tract dilation. Ask which question each test answers and how its result would change care.

Follow-up depends on one- or two-sided disease

With unilateral dysplasia, clinicians generally arrange at least yearly follow-up to check for problems such as high blood pressure or urine protein, even when the child feels well. Blood tests and repeat ultrasound are selected according to the remaining kidney, urinary findings, age and previous results. A reassuring first scan does not end future monitoring.

Bilateral dysplasia usually needs closer kidney-specialist follow-up continuing into adulthood. Blood pressure, urine protein, growth, kidney-function blood tests and imaging are reviewed more often, especially in infancy or when results change. The schedule is individualized; do not apply a single scan interval to everyone. Ask who reviews each result and how follow-up will continue through puberty and adult care.

Treatment protects the function that remains

No medicine can rebuild a dysplastic kidney into a normally developed one. A well child with adequate function may need monitoring rather than an operation. If problems occur, care can include treatment of infection or high blood pressure, assessment of reflux or obstruction, and kidney-disease support tailored to the child. Do not start antibiotics, supplements or a kidney-cleansing remedy without advice.

Removing a dysplastic kidney is not routine. For example, a poorly functioning kidney with blood pressure that cannot otherwise be controlled may need a surgical discussion. The team weighs the actual complication, remaining function and risks. Food and fluid advice also depends on function and growth: avoid imposing a restrictive diet or forcing extra water. Reduced function may require a paediatric kidney dietitian and an individual feeding plan.

When both kidneys are severely affected

Some babies need specialist support soon after birth, particularly if very low amniotic fluid affected lung development or kidney function is severely reduced. Others with bilateral dysplasia have no immediate crisis and are monitored over years. Neither an automatic fatal outcome nor a promise of normal lifelong function is justified by the word bilateral alone.

If kidney failure develops, dialysis and later assessment for transplantation may be needed. These are planned by an experienced paediatric kidney team according to the baby's size, health and other needs; transplantation is not an automatic immediate newborn treatment. Ask about the expected benefits, burdens, uncertainty, breathing support where relevant and all appropriate care options, including comfort-focused support in very severe circumstances.

Growing up and keeping a practical care plan

Many children with adequate overall function can attend school, play and take part in ordinary life. Keep reports and a written plan for appointments, medicines, illness and who to contact. Symptoms are not a reliable substitute for blood-pressure and kidney-health checks. Ask for emotional support if the uncertainty feels overwhelming.

Tell healthcare professionals about the kidney condition before new medicines or procedures. Check nonprescription products with the team, particularly during vomiting or dehydration. As the child grows, involve them in understanding their diagnosis and follow-up. Family planning or a future pregnancy may warrant specialist review, without assuming one recurrence estimate or outcome fits every family.

Illness should not wait for the next kidney appointment

Seek urgent same-day medical advice for possible urinary infection, blood in urine, poor feeding, repeated vomiting or fewer wet nappies, and mention the kidney history. Suspected UTI in a baby under three months needs immediate paediatric assessment. Follow any more specific illness instructions from the child's team; urine appearance alone cannot confirm or exclude infection.

Get emergency help for difficulty breathing, a seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, difficulty waking, or suspected infection with confusion, unusual drowsiness or difficulty speaking. In children under five, no urine for twelve hours, unusual pallor or blue/grey skin, a temperature below 36°C, or 38°C or higher in a baby under three months also needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not wait for every sign or for twelve hours if the child is already seriously unwell. Do not drive yourself in an emergency; arrange another driver or an ambulance.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the team to explain the exact kidney diagnosis, remaining function, other urinary findings and any uncertainty on prenatal or postnatal imaging.

Keep a written plan for blood pressure, urine, growth, blood tests and selected imaging; ask whether genetics advice or a kidney dietitian is relevant, without adding treatments yourself.

Learn the child's illness instructions and urgent contacts. Seek care for warning signs rather than waiting for the next scan or an app reminder.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organize appointments, clinician-provided results, feeding or urine observations and questions for the kidney team. It cannot interpret a scan, estimate kidney function, diagnose infection or decide that a sick baby can wait. Clinical warning signs take priority over logging.

When to seek help

Follow the child's individual kidney and illness plan. Suspected UTI under three months requires immediate paediatric assessment. Breathing difficulty, seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, difficulty waking or infection with confusion, unusual drowsiness or difficulty speaking requires emergency care. Under five, no urine for twelve hours, unusual pallor/blue-grey skin or a temperature below 36°C is also an emergency; under three months, 38°C or higher needs emergency assessment. Seek help sooner if already seriously unwell. Do not drive yourself in an emergency. Do not add antibiotics, supplements or restrictive feeding changes without clinical advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Kidney dysplasia can affect part or all of one or both kidneys; remaining function varies.
  • MCDK, hypoplasia, an absent kidney and inherited polycystic disease are not interchangeable diagnoses.
  • Scans, selected tests and a written follow-up plan matter even when the baby seems well.
  • Treatment addresses actual complications; routine removal, restrictive diets and guaranteed outcomes are inappropriate.
  • Seek help promptly for infection or new illness; emergency warning signs override app tracking and routine appointments.

Frequently asked questions

What does dysplasia on my baby's scan mean?

It suggests that kidney tissue developed abnormally. The team needs to explain whether one or both kidneys are affected, how certain the diagnosis is, the urinary-tract findings and what is known about function. It does not automatically mean that a kidney is absent or that all function is lost.

What symptoms can it cause?

Many affected babies have no obvious symptoms. Blood pressure, urine protein or function can change silently; urinary infections and poor growth or feeding may also need assessment. An enlarged painful kidney can occur in some cystic cases but is not universal. Keep planned checks rather than relying only on symptoms.

What causes kidney dysplasia?

Often no precise cause is found. Genetic or wider developmental conditions and certain exposures can be relevant, but the finding alone does not establish parental fault or an individual medicine as the cause. Family history, other findings and specialist counselling guide testing and future-pregnancy advice.

What treatment does a newborn need?

That depends on function, both kidneys and associated problems. Some babies need monitoring only; others need treatment for infection, blood pressure, drainage difficulties or reduced kidney function. Severe disease may need neonatal support and kidney replacement treatment. An operation is not routine for every dysplastic kidney.

Is all kidney dysplasia MCDK?

No. MCDK is a severe cystic form with little or no useful function in the affected kidney. Broader dysplasia may have no cysts or retain some function. Other small-kidney and cystic conditions need to be distinguished by specialists.

Will both dysplastic kidneys fail at birth?

Not necessarily. Some babies have enough function initially and may not need dialysis for years, while others have serious early problems. Growth and previous results influence follow-up. No single scan label can guarantee the course or determine an individual survival prediction.

Does a well child still need follow-up?

Yes. Blood pressure and urine protein can change before symptoms. Unilateral disease generally needs yearly review, while bilateral disease usually needs closer specialist checks through childhood and adulthood. Blood tests and imaging are tailored to findings; ask for the actual schedule.

When should we seek urgent help?

Possible UTI, blood in urine, poor feeding, repeated vomiting or fewer wet nappies need urgent advice; suspected UTI under three months needs immediate paediatric assessment. Breathing difficulty, seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, difficulty waking, or infection with confusion, unusual drowsiness or speech difficulty need emergency help. Under five, no urine for twelve hours, unusual pale/blue-grey skin or below 36°C is also an emergency; under three months, 38°C or higher needs emergency care. Seek help sooner if seriously unwell and do not drive yourself in an emergency.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
